text: What on earth are rhetorical goals? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion and I am fond
of talking about rhetorical goals. And that just refers to the goals of someone's rhetoric. So what is rhetoric?
Well, that is the art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing. So it is
crafting speech or texts in order to maximize the likelihood that they will accomplish what you want them to
accomplish. And so when it comes to the Bible, every single syllable of the Bible was written in order to serve some
kind of rhetorical goal or some combination of rhetorical goals. And no, it was not to just transmit information.
The Bible is not this found footage, a kind of verbatim account of things that happened and things that were said.
Everything in the Bible was crafted literarily in order to achieve the rhetorical goals of the authors. And
every author had a different set of rhetorical goals. So in order to best interpret what the authors were trying to say, we need to understand what they
were trying to do. And that's kind of a feedback loop. You don't establish one and then establish the other. You work towards a better understanding by using
each to inform your interpretation of the other. So when I talk about the rhetorical goals of the authors, I'm
talking about what scholars think they were most likely trying to achieve. And that might have to do with structuring power or values or boundaries. It might
have to do with asserting or altering authoritative knowledge. It might have to do with challenging somebody else's
assertion of authoritative knowledge or identities or something like that. There are all kinds of different things that
authors could be trying to do with their texts. And if we ignore those, then we're not going to have a good chance of
reconstructing what made those texts meaningful and useful to them. Instead,
we're overwhelmingly going to subordinate the text to our own rhetorical goals. What we want the text to do for us, what will make them
meaningful and useful to us. At which point, we're not following the Bible.
We're leading the Bible. We're showing the Bible where it is going to go, what it is going to do, and what it is and is
not allowed to say. So, if we don't take seriously the rhetorical goals of the authors, we're not going to take seriously the Bible. We're just going to
try to leverage the Bible to serve our own rhetorical goals. And that brings up a final point. You should understand why
you're reading the Bible, why you're engaging it, what your own rhetorical goals are. And the better you understand
those, the better you can determine which methods and which hermeneutic lenses and things like that to bring to
the Bible to best serve those rhetorical goals. And if your rhetorical goals are to use the Bible to structure power and
values and boundaries over and against the interests of minoritized or marginalized or oppressed groups, don't
do that. And the fit for this video is for all those who are not into the whole brevity thing.
